name: Carrasca Milenaria de Lecina
species: Holm Oak, the carrasca/ballota form (Quercus ilex subsp. ballota)

location.address: Beside the street next to the cemetery wall of the church, Lecina, Barcabo, Huesca province, Aragon

access: Free, publicly accessible. A short walk (about four minutes) from the village centre along a path bordered by stone walls, past an old threshing ground; protective barriers stand at the base to keep foot traffic off the root plate, but the tree itself is not fenced off from view or from a close approach. Guided visits are also organised via parqueculturalriovero.com.
transport: Rural village in the Sierra de Guara / Sobrarbe area of Huesca; no confirmed public transport to Lecina, reachable by car.
verify_notes: Alive and actively cared for: the tree's own dedicated site (lacarrascadelecina.com) documents ongoing 2021 stewardship and events under its canopy ('Seguiremos cuidando nuestra carrasca 1000 anos mas'). Species confirmed to subspecies level via Wikidata (Quercus ilex subsp. ballota), which is the taxon Spanish calls 'carrasca'. Sources agree it is one of Spain's largest and oldest holm oaks: height 16.5m (Wikipedia/own site) vs 16.26m (Wikidata), crown diameter 28m, crown area 615 sq m -- all three sources agree closely on these. FLAGGED for two numeric conflicts, neither large enough to doubt the tree but real disagreements: (1) girth/perimeter given as 610cm on Spanish Wikipedia and its own site's base-diameter figure (1.75m base diameter, consistent with a girth around 5.5-6m), but Wikidata's own P2043 statement gives perimeter as 700cm -- recorded girth_cm as the more specific 610cm from Wikipedia, note the 700cm alternative for the writer. (2) age: Wikipedia and the tree's own site both plainly state 'edad estimada de 1100 anos' / 'aproximadamente 1000 anos' with no dendrochronological study cited (i.e. this is a round, traditional estimate rather than a derived one); a WebSearch AI summary claimed a dendrochronology-based dispute putting the real age at 500-600 years, but that claim was NOT found on any directly fetched page (including the Wikipedia article itself) and is discarded per the search-summary-is-not-a-source rule -- it may exist on a source not yet checked, so a future pass should look at Aragon's own catalogo de arboles singulares before repeating '1000 years' as settled. Recognition: European Tree of the Year 2021 (with a record 104,264 votes) and Spain's Tree of the Year 2020; included in Aragon's catalogue of singular trees. This is clearly a destination tree in its own right (would somebody travel specifically for this one tree: yes, it has its own tourism campaign and a website). Two independent sources used: Spanish Wikipedia and the tree's own dedicated site (lacarrascadelecina.com, run by the local cultural park), cross-checked against Wikidata Q109316184 whose coordinates (42 13'47.06"N, 0 02'18.46"E) convert to exactly the brief's coordinate, confirming tree-level pin precision.

name: Encina Tres Patas de Mendaza

location.address: Paraje de La Laguna, on the east slope of the Dos Hermanas hill, between Mendaza and the Ermita de Santa Coloma, Mendaza, Navarre

access: Free, open countryside. Reached on foot along the path between Mendaza village and the Ermita de Santa Coloma; a waymarked circular hiking route (confirmed via a published Wikiloc track) passes the tree. No indication anywhere of private land or restricted access.
transport: Rural, in Navarre's Berrueza valley; no public transport confirmed to Mendaza, reachable by car. Nearest town of any size is Estella-Lizarra.
verify_notes: Alive and in good condition: Spanish Wikipedia states plainly 'Muestra un excelente estado y vitalidad' (shows excellent condition and vitality), noting metal bands were fitted around the hollow trunk to stop it splitting open, a maintenance intervention rather than a decline sign. Famous for its structure: the trunk is entirely hollow and stands on three thick buttress 'legs' (the name means 'Three-Legged Oak'), with a 1.4m-high hollow between them per one source. Numbers agree cleanly across all sources with no conflict: perimeter/girth 770cm, height 15.5m, crown diameter 19.2m, coordinates (Wikidata 42 38'35.1"N 2 13'55.7"W converts to exactly the brief's pin, confirming tree-level precision). Declared a Natural Monument by the Government of Navarre in 1991 (Foral Decree 165/1991, per Wikipedia) and included in Navarre's Catalogo de Arboles Monumentales; won Spain's national 'arbol mas longevo' prize from the Ministry of Environment in 2007 and was a top-10 finalist for European Tree of the Year 2020 (per Wikidata and escapadarural.com). Age of 'roughly 1200 years' / 'segundo arbol mas longevo de Espana' (second-oldest tree in Spain) is repeated consistently across every source with no dendrochronological study cited, so it is a repeated traditional estimate rather than a derived figure; treated as an honest round-number estimate rather than sharpened further. Site has a documented history: the ground was the scene of an 1837 Carlist-war skirmish (the Battle of Mendaza) per the search summary, not yet independently verified on a fetched page, so leave that anecdote for the writer to verify further before using it. Destination test: yes, a national award-winner and European Tree of the Year finalist with its own hiking route and multiple dedicated write-ups; would clearly draw a visit for itself. monumentaltrees.com record exists (13009_ermitadesantacoloma/25092) but 403'd automated fetch as expected per the rulebook; not used, not needed given two solid independent sources already.

name: Olmos Centenarios de la Ermita de Belen (the Centenary Elms of Cabeza del Buey)

location.address: Santuario de Nuestra Senora de Belen, Ctra. EX-104, about 11 km from Cabeza del Buey (3 km from Almorchon), Badajoz province, Extremadura
location.neighbourhood: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Belen

access: Free, open. The elms stand in the grounds of a working pilgrimage sanctuary beside a public road (EX-104), the site of an annual pilgrimage every 27 September since at least 1650/1723; the trees themselves are ringed with protective wooden railings to keep visitors off the roots, but the grounds are open and there is no gate or admission charge mentioned anywhere.
transport: Rural, off the EX-104 road, 11 km from Cabeza del Buey and 3 km from Almorchon; no public transport confirmed, reachable by car.
verify_notes: ENSEMBLE JUDGEMENT (the key open question for this candidate): this is seven Ulmus minor elms clustered together in the grounds of a single hermitage/sanctuary (Nuestra Senora de Belen), not a scattered group or a roadside avenue. Three independent descriptions agree it reads as one compact site rather than a spread-out population: the municipal site (cabezadelbuey.es) calls it 'los siete olmos centenarios' positioned 'en el entorno de la ermita'; Wikipedia calls it 'un conjunto de olmos... situado en el entorno de la ermita'; and a travel blog (fotonazos.es) describes them as 'located together as a cohesive group' within 'an enormous complex with lush grass under a good canopy of trees', i.e. the sanctuary courtyard itself is the one obvious place to stand, the same shape as the Lomanstraat tunnel precedent (a compact, famous ensemble with a single viewing point) rather than the disqualified La Rambla plane-tree case. Judged: QUALIFIES as one collectible point. Alive: confirmed as 'one of the few living elm groves in Spain that has survived Dutch elm disease (grafiosis)', per Wikipedia and the municipal site both; some trunks are hollowed by past disease damage and the grove has been cordoned and propped (acordonados y apuntalados) to keep it standing, which is a conservation intervention, not a death signal. Official designation: declared Arboles Singulares de Extremadura by the Junta de Extremadura, Decreto 140/2005 (confirmed via WebSearch summary of the official designation, consistent across two sources; the primary decree text itself was not fetched directly, only cited by secondary sources, so this is recorded as an official designation from secondary citation rather than a primary-document read). Named Spain's Tree of the Year 2017 (per turismocabezadelbuey.com) and placed 2nd in European Tree of the Year 2018 with 22,323 votes (per the initial WebSearch summary, corroborated independently by the municipal site's separate mention of the 2018 contest). Only one height figure exists: 14m for one specimen (Wikipedia, municipal site) vs a looser 'about 20 metres with their branches' from the travel blog for the grove generally, not treated as a conflict since one is a stated single-tree figure and the other a loose visual impression of the canopy; no girth/circumference figure found anywhere despite searching the municipal site, Wikipedia, redex.org (301-redirected, dead link) and turismoextremadura.com (site returned 'servicio no disponible', both after a first attempt, not retried further per the two-attempts rule) -- girth_cm left null, a real data gap for a future pass or reader to close. Location precision: pin taken from a Wikimedia Commons photographer's own geotag on the file '2018_Ancient_elms_of_Cabeza_Buey_ES.jpg' (38 42'20.59"N 5 19'26.54"W), which converts to exactly the brief's coordinate and was shot at the grove itself (categorised under this exact tree group), so treated as confirmed for an ensemble in the same way a mapped photo confirms a single tree. Destination test: yes -- a national award-winning, historically significant elm grove (one of the last of its kind in Spain, tied to a pilgrimage tradition since the 17th century) is a genuine reason to make the trip on its own.

name: Urkietako Artea (Encina de Urkieta)

location.address: Barrio de San Roman / crossroads toward Besangiz, Muxika, Biscay, Basque Country (opposite Muxika railway station, off the BI-6315 Amorebieta-Gernika road)

access: Free, open. Stands beside a public road/crossroads in the San Roman district, reached by turning off the BI-6315 regional road near Muxika train station and continuing about 2km through the neighbourhood; no source mentions any gate, fee or restriction.
transport: Muxika station (Euskotren line E4, Bilbao-Matiko to Bermeo/Mundaka) sits right by the turning to the tree, with direct trains from central Bilbao every 30 minutes on weekdays. HONEST TRAVEL TIME, checked because this candidate sits close-ish to Bilbao: the journey is roughly 45-50 minutes by train (Bilbao-Gernika, one stop further, runs 49-54 minutes over 21km on this branch line), which is past the ~30-minute day-trip boundary this project uses for folding a tree into an existing city's page. Straight-line distance is about 18.5km, but the rail line is a slow regional/coastal branch with many stops, so the real time is the honest figure to use, not the distance.
verify_notes: PLACEMENT JUDGEMENT (the key open question for this candidate): does NOT clear the ~30-minute public-transport day-trip boundary for being folded into Bilbao as a day-trip entry (real journey time is 45-50 minutes each way by direct train, not the roughly 30 minutes the rule asks for), despite being closer as the crow flies (18.5km) than many of our confirmed day-trips elsewhere. Flagging this rather than deciding it, since 'is this worth its own page given very low measured demand (4 reads/month across 1 language, per the brief)' is a publish-priority judgement, not a verification one, and a judgement call about whether a tree is good enough must never block delivery of the facts. Recorded here as a verified tree either way. Alive and in good condition: both sources describe an actively admired, well-formed specimen with no disease or decline mentioned; 2021-dated Commons photograph (categorised precisely as this tree) shows a full, healthy crown. Species confirmed as Quercus ilex subsp. ilex (the same species as Lecina's carrasca above, different subspecies -- ilex rather than ballota, consistent with the more Atlantic/northern Basque climate versus Lecina's dry inland Aragon). Officially protected: declared a singular tree under the Basque Country's nature conservation law by Decreto 265/1995, de 16 de Mayo (Basque Government), and it is one of only two centenarian holm oaks recorded in Biscay province (the other in Garai, itself already a lead in data/leads/_famous-spain.json). Measurements agree across both sources: total height 12m, crown diameter 26m, trunk height before branching only 1.5m (the tree was historically pruned to grow wide rather than tall, which the low branching and 26m crown both corroborate). REGISTER PITFALL CAUGHT: one WebFetch summary of the floresyplantas.net page mislabelled the trunk measurement as 'Diameter at 1.30m = 4.3 metres' (which would be a physically implausible ~13.5m circumference); re-fetching the actual underlying blog text showed the real figure is 'Perimetro a 1,3m (d): 4,3 metros', i.e. a circumference/girth of 430cm at breast height, not a diameter -- recorded girth_cm as 430, the corrected figure. No age figure exists in either source and none is derivable responsibly: no published Quercus ilex growth-rate figure was found and record to hand, and inventing one from girth alone would be exactly the fabrication this rulebook forbids, so age_estimate is left empty for the page to ask the reader. Location precision: pin taken from a geotagged Commons photograph of this exact named tree (43 16'53.9"N 2 42'37.22"W), which converts to exactly the brief's coordinate. Destination test: honestly weaker than the other three candidates -- no national or European tree-of-the-year recognition, just a local government protection decree and appearances in a couple of dedicated landscape/nature blogs; whether that clears the bar for its own single-tree page (as opposed to staying a lead) is a call for whoever assembles the site, not settled here.
